claim: pam_systemd launches a per-user systemd --user instance at the user's first login; it is killed when the user's last session closes unless lingering (loginctl enable-linger) is enabled, in which case the instance starts at boot and persists
stance_target: user-scoped agents on headless hosts require lingering — the default user-manager lifecycle kills them at last logout
quoted_support: As per default configuration in /etc/pam.d/system-login, the pam_systemd module automatically launches a systemd --user instance when the user logs in for the first time. This process will survive as long as there is some session for that user, and will be killed as soon as the last session for the user is closed. When #Automatic start-up of systemd user instances is enabled, the instance is started on boot and will not be killed.

claim: The systemd --user instance is per-user, NOT per-session: all user services run outside of any login session, so programs that need to run inside a session will probably break in user services
stance_target: session-bound functionality (e.g. desktop-session integration) cannot be assumed available to a lingered user-service agent
quoted_support: Be aware that the systemd --user instance is a per-user process, and not per-session ... This means that all user services run outside of a session. As a consequence, programs that need to be run inside a session will probably break in user services.

claim: User units CANNOT reference or depend on system units or on units of other users
stance_target: an agent running as a user service cannot order itself after system-level units — a structural constraint on user-service deployment
quoted_support: User units can not reference or depend on system units or units of other users.

claim: User units inherit NO shell environment (.bashrc etc.); environment must be injected via ~/.config/environment.d/*.conf, /etc/systemd/user.conf DefaultEnvironment, drop-ins under /etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d/, systemctl --user set-environment/import-environment, dbus-update-activation-environment --systemd --all, or a systemd.environment-generator(7) script; the user manager only reads env vars set at its start (upstream bug #29414, closed WONTFIX)
stance_target: an agent's env-var strategy (XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS, PATH) must be declared via these mechanisms, not assumed from login profiles
quoted_support: Units started by user instance of systemd do not inherit any of the environment variables set in places like .bashrc etc. ... the systemd user instance will only use environment variables that are set when it is started. In particular, it will not try parsing files, see upstream bug #29414 (closed WONTFIX).

claim: User-unit search path in ascending precedence: /usr/lib/systemd/user/ → ~/.local/share/systemd/user/ → /etc/systemd/user/ → ~/.config/systemd/user/; 'systemctl --global enable' installs for all users; %h expands to the running user's home
stance_target: unit placement and precedence rules a fleet agent's installer must respect
quoted_support: user units are located in the following directories (ordered by ascending precedence): /usr/lib/systemd/user/ ... ~/.local/share/systemd/user/ ... /etc/systemd/user/ ... ~/.config/systemd/user/ ... If you want to enable a unit for all users rather than the user executing the systemctl command, run systemctl --global enable unit as root.

claim: Warning: systemd services run outside of logind — do not use lingering to enable automatic login, as it breaks the session; journald does not write separate user journals for UIDs below 1000 (everything goes to the system journal)
stance_target: operational constraints (no session semantics; low-UID users' logs land in the system journal) for fleet agent user design
quoted_support: Warning systemd services are not sessions, they run outside of logind. Do not use lingering to enable automatic login as it will break the session. ... Note journald will not write user journals for users with UIDs below 1000, instead directing everything to the system journal.
